name: Cope / copium

lead: 'Cope' is forum slang for something people tell themselves to feel better. In looksmaxxing it is used to sort methods into those considered real and those considered wishful; in blackpill spaces it is also aimed at self-improvement and personality itself.

Calling something cope marks it as self-deceptive and tends to end discussion of whether it might help. On tier lists, low-rated methods such as thumbpulling are labelled this way. It is slang for argument, not a technique, and researchers have not studied the term directly.

paras: People use it in forum replies and tier lists, aimed at others' claims or at their own reassurances, and it influences which methods get attention.
Communities that use it heavily are linked in studies with fatalistic beliefs and mental-health burdens. The word itself has no documented physical risk.

chain: Shapes what people try for looks
angle.text: Forum users apply 'cope' to sort looksmaxxing methods into those they consider real and those they consider wishful, which shapes what people end up trying for their looks. Blackpill users also apply it to self-improvement itself. It is slang for argument, not a technique.

lead: 'Cope' and its jokey form 'copium' are online slang for something a person tells themselves to feel better about an unwelcome reality. In looksmaxxing, incel and blackpill communities the word works as a filter: members label a method, a belief or an argument 'cope' to signal that they expect it not to change how someone looks or is seen. [1][2][3]

The term shapes how people choose what to try. Methods ranked as 'cope' on forum tier lists, such as thumbpulling, are set aside, while methods ranked as 'not cope' (skincare, body-fat reduction, hair, surgery and other changes to visible features) receive most of the attention. Members use the label to steer each other toward changes they expect to show in the mirror or in photos. [2][4]

Outside looksmaxxing the word has a wider life. Know Your Meme traces 'copium' to a 2003 album title and to 4chan posts in 2018 and 2019, and records that 'cope' spread through Urban Dictionary, imageboards, Twitter and political commentary around 2019 and 2020. Dictionaries define it as slang for a delusion or coping mechanism. [5][6][7]

The word is also used reflexively: users describe their own reassurance, such as telling themselves they look better than they fear, as 'cope'. No academic study of the word itself has been published; research on the surrounding communities, including a 2025 sociological analysis of a looksmaxxing forum, is described below.

paras: In incel and blackpill discourse, 'cope' labels optimism or self-improvement as self-deception, and a believer might call anything from a personality-based strategy to a skincare routine 'cope'. [1] Wikipedia's article on incels describes the blackpill as a fatalistic ideology holding that attractiveness is largely determined by genetics, which is the setting in which dismissing hopeful strategies as 'cope' is most common. [3]

In looksmaxxing, Grokipedia describes the term as dismissing a method as ineffective or self-deceptive, and gives thumbpulling as an example that tier lists rank low. [2] Forum threads such as 'cope vs not cope 2024 looksmax list' show members sorting practices into the two groups and explaining their reasoning. [4]

The word turns up in many forms: 'coping' as a verb, 'copium' as a joke substance members say they are inhaling, and 'cope' as a charge aimed at another user's claim about their own looks, for example when someone rates themselves higher than others do. [8] Wiktionary lists the general senses of 'copium' as a metaphorical opiate taken to deal with loss or disillusionment, and as a naive coping mechanism for facts a person knows are untrue. [7]

Wiktionary describes 'copium' as a blend of 'cope' and 'opium' and cites a 2003 album titled Copium by the rapper Keak da Sneak as the earliest use. [7] Know Your Meme gives the same album (released 17 June 2003) and adds an anonymous 4chan post using the word on the /int/ board on 30 March 2018, followed by a /pol/ post on 5 July 2019 of the Pepe the Frog image inhaling 'copium' from a gas tank. [5]

The same page records that the image spread in 2020: a 9GAG post in June, a Reddit post in August that drew more than 1,200 points, and a September 2020 tweet by the YouTuber Vaush captioned 'Trump rn'. On 3 October 2020 an Urban Dictionary user defined copium as a metaphorical opiate inhaled when faced with loss, failure or defeat, especially in sports and politics. [5]

For 'cope' itself, Know Your Meme reports that an Urban Dictionary user added a definition on 9 August 2019 describing it as a term used by 'looksmaxing incels' to call a strategy invalid. It notes the phrase spread on 4chan in summer 2019 alongside 'copium', that it became the punchline of a 'Cancelling Plans Is OK' snowclone on Twitter in January 2020, and that use rose around the 2020 US election, with an @RightWingCope account launched in November 2020 that gained more than 205,000 followers in four months. [6]

Know Your Meme lists earlier phrases as precursors, including a 2005 webcomic phrase and a December 2016 Tumblr format that mocked unusual self-care routines. [6] Wikipedia's incel article records the community's own timeline, including the 2017 ban of r/incels and the 2019 ban of r/braincels, after which discussion moved to dedicated forums. [3]

Tier lists are the clearest example. Threads rank methods into 'cope' and 'not cope' columns, and members argue over placements such as height-increase exercises, jaw exercisers, skincare, hair treatments, weight loss, surgery and hormones. [4] Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing describes the community's tier lists, rating scales and terminology, including the softmaxxing and hardmaxxing split that 'cope' lists often follow. [9]

Grokipedia describes the label as applying both to techniques seen as lacking evidence and to blackpill-adjacent views that dismiss personality or effort. [2] Some members present sorting methods this way as a way to concentrate effort on interventions with visible results, while others describe it as gatekeeping. [2]

Because members apply the word to claims about height, face structure and surgery alike, what counts as 'cope' differs across threads and over time. Some posters write that 'cope' can be a useful state of mind; others use it as an insult. [8]

Users also apply the word to themselves. One looksmax.org poster describes telling themselves they look better as 'cope' that collapses periodically, illustrating how the word can describe both external arguments and internal reassurance.

Other threads use 'cope' in its ordinary psychological sense; one poster, for instance, describes trying to cope with a facial feature they dislike and asks which softmaxxing or hardmaxxing options might help, showing that the word also covers managing feelings about appearance. [10]
Grokipedia notes that the fatalism behind much 'cope' language rests on evolutionary and dating-data arguments that it says overgeneralise short-term mating research. [1]

A 2025 study in Sociology of Health & Illness by Michael Halpin and colleagues qualitatively analysed 8,072 comments from a looksmaxxing forum with about six million monthly visitors. The authors report that users critique men's bodies through a hegemonic masculine lens, that the community encourages drastic body changes such as leg-lengthening surgery and mewing, and that users experience 'masculine demoralisation'. They conclude that such communities can harm participants' health.

Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing records commentators' concerns about body dysmorphia and the judgemental tone of the community, as well as some practitioners' reports of social benefits. It does not discuss the word 'cope' specifically. [9]

The ADL, as quoted in Wikipedia, distinguishes 'redpilled' incels who try to improve their looks from 'blackpilled' ones who regard improvement as futile. 'Cope' is the vocabulary that marks that boundary in everyday forum talk. [3]
